{{Short description|Canadian-American physicist (1929–2016)}}
'''Gordon Thompson Danby''' (November 8, 1929 – August 2, 2016) was a Canadian-American physicist notable (together with Dr. [[James R. Powell (physicist)|James R. Powell]]) for his work on superconducting [[Maglev (transport)|Maglev]], for which he shared the [[Benjamin Franklin Medal (Franklin Institute)|Franklin Institute 'Medal 2000 for Engineering']].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Obituary: Gordon T. Danby |url=https://bera.bnl.gov/brea/wp-content/uploads/sites/22/2021/08/Danby-Gordon.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="NYT">{{Cite news |last=Fountain |first=Henry |date=2016-08-12 |title=Gordon T. Danby, Who Helped Invent Magnetic-Levitation Trains, Dies at 86 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/08/12/science/gordon-t-danby-dies-at-86-helped-invent-magnetic-levitation-trains.html |access-date=2026-04-23 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.sciamdigital.com/index.cfm?fa=Products.ViewIssuePreview&ARTICLEID_CHAR=F8FA1649-9242-47A4-AE1E-7C0E0229B53 |title=Maglev: A New Approach |access-date=2010-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120305162125/http://www.sciamdigital.com/index.cfm?fa=Products.ViewIssuePreview&ARTICLEID_CHAR=F8FA1649-9242-47A4-AE1E-7C0E0229B53 |archive-date=2012-03-05 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uwEAAAAAMBAJ&q=powell+danby&pg=PA78|title=Popular Science|first=Bonnier|last=Corporation|date=June 29, 1992|publisher=Bonnier Corporation|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maglev2000.com/company/about-04-c.html |title=Maglev 2000 |access-date=2010-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110125233242/http://www.maglev2000.com/company/about-04-c.html |archive-date=2011-01-25 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Danby was born in [[Richmond,_Ontario|Richmond]], Ontario (now part of [[Ottawa]]) and went to [[Carleton University]] to study mathematics and physics before going to [[McGill University]] in Montreal, where he received a PhD in 1956. He started working at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] on Long Island, New York the following year and continued working there until 1999.<ref name="NYT"/> Danby was responsible for designing the magnetic storage ring initially used for E821 at BNL, which was later moved to Fermilab for the [[Muon g-2]] experiment.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Morse and Roberts Win W.K.H. Panofsky Prize for Muon g-2 Experiment |url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=120864 |access-date=2026-04-23 |website=Brookhaven National Laboratory |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1063/1.1372101|title = Have We Glimpsed 'New Physics' in the Muon's Anomalous Magnetic Moment?|year = 2001|last1 = Schwarzschild|first1 = Bertram|journal = Physics Today|volume = 54|issue = 4|pages = 18–20|bibcode = 2001PhT....54d..18S|doi-access = free}}</ref> He was devoted to his wife Jane, and was personally known for his warmth and compassion.
